kzz7yh-f124550-d1e103.summary: Announces two questions on the second principal topic, the power of ruling.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e112.summary: First question: whether every power of ruling is from God.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e117.summary: Second question: whether there would have been lordship or prelacy in the state of innocence.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e126.summary: First objection: Hosea 8 says of some, 'they have reigned, but not by me'; so not every ruling power is from God.
claims: Some kings reign without God (objection).

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e142.summary: Second objection: some rule by usurped power, and nothing usurped, being unjustly taken, is from God.
claims: Usurped power is not from God (objection).

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e149.summary: Third objection: no power from God is to be resisted, but the devil's power must be resisted (James 4), so his rule over evil men and angels is not from God.
claims: The devil's power must be resisted (objection).

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e160.summary: Sed contra from Romans 13: there is no power except from God.
claims: All power is from God.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e166.summary: Second sed contra: Job 34 says God makes a hypocrite reign because of the people's sins, so even wicked rule is from God, and a fortiori that of the good.
claims: God sets even wicked rulers over sinful peoples.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e177.summary: Richard's solution distinguishes three aspects of ruling power: its essence, its mode of acquisition and its mode of use. The essence is an order of superior to inferior, always good and instituted by God for praising the good and punishing evildoers (Romans 13). Just acquisition is from God and unjust acquisition only by permission. Likewise good use is from God and evil use only by permission.
claims: The essence of ruling power is a God-instituted order of superior to inferior.
Unjust acquisition and abuse of power are from God only permissively.
Ruling power exists for praising the good and punishing evildoers.
concepts: essence, acquisition and use of power

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e206.summary: Reply to Hosea: it concerns power as to its illicit mode of acquisition.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e215.summary: Reply to the usurpation objection: the usurper's mode of acquiring is not from God, yet the same power is sometimes conferred on him by God; one and the same power is usurped with respect to the man and justly conferred with respect to God, which is consistent under different respects.
claims: The same power can be usurped by a person and justly conferred by God under different respects.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e233.summary: Reply to the devil objection: what must be resisted is the devil's abuse of his power in luring people to sin, which abuse is not from God.
claims: Resistance is owed to the abuse of power, not to power as such.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e242.summary: The sed contra arguments hold of power with respect to its essence.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e253.summary: First argument for lordship in innocence: the man is head of the woman (1 Cor 11), and there were man and woman in innocence.
claims: Headship of man over woman existed in innocence (argument).

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e266.summary: Second argument: holy angels have lordship and prelacy, as their names (principalities, powers, dominations) show, so likewise humans in innocence.
claims: Angelic hierarchy includes dominion (argument).

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e277.summary: Third argument: right reason places the wiser and better over the less wise and good; in innocence not all would have been equal in prudence and goodness.
claims: Inequality of prudence would have warranted rule in innocence (argument).

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e295.summary: Sed contra from Augustine (City of God 19.15): God willed rational man made in his image to rule only irrational creatures, not man over man.
claims: God did not intend man to rule man.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e309.summary: Second sed contra: lordship implies servitude, and Augustine says servitude was imposed rightly because of sin.
claims: Servitude is a consequence of sin.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e318.summary: Richard's solution distinguishes three senses of lordship. In the broadest sense, ownership of what one uses at will, it would have existed in innocence. In a narrower sense, the power to command another person, it would have existed in husband over wife and parents over children, which belongs to nature as instituted and not only as fallen. In the proper sense, coercive power, which involves acting against the subject's will or inclination or punishing for evil, it belongs only to fallen nature: it was absent in innocence and will be absent in glory, when all prelacy ceases (gloss on 1 Cor 15).
claims: Dominion as use and as directive command would have existed in innocence.
Wifely and filial obedience belong to nature as instituted.
Coercive dominion exists only because of the Fall and will cease in glory.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e411.summary: The first argument (headship) holds of dominion in the second sense, the power to command.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e366.summary: The angelic hierarchy argument is solved likewise, as concerning non-coercive dominion.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e368.summary: Reply to the third argument: though unequal in prudence and goodness, each person in innocence would have had enough, with divine help, to govern himself; so there would have been no coercive dominion, and directive dominion only of husband over wife and parents over children.
claims: In innocence each person, with divine help, could govern himself.
Directive dominion in innocence was limited to the household.

kzz7yh-f124550-d1e386.summary: The Augustinian sed contra arguments hold of dominion in the third, coercive sense.

kzz7yh-f124550-Dd1e122.summary: Question 1 holds that every ruling power is from God as to its essence, an order of superior to inferior instituted for praising the good and punishing evildoers. Its acquisition and use are from God only when just and good; when unjust or evil they are from God only by permission. So the kings of Hosea who 'reigned not by me' acquired power illicitly. A usurped power can at once be wrongly seized by the person and justly conferred by God. What we must resist in the devil is his abuse of power, not the power itself.
claims: All ruling power is from God in its essence.
Unjust acquisition and abuse are only permitted by God.
One may resist abuse of power without resisting power as such.

kzz7yh-f124550-Dd1e249.summary: Question 2 asks whether lordship would have existed in the state of innocence and answers by distinguishing three senses of dominium. Ownership and use of things would have existed. Directive command would have existed too, though only of husband over wife and parents over children, since such household obedience belongs to nature as instituted. Coercive dominion, which acts against the subject's will or punishes, exists only because of the Fall and will cease in glory. The scriptural and angelic arguments concern directive dominion, Augustine's denial concerns coercive dominion, and unequal prudence would not have required rule since each could govern himself with God's help.
claims: Coercive political dominion is a consequence of the Fall.
Directive household authority belongs to unfallen nature.
All prelacy will cease in glory.

kzz7yh-f124550.summary: Article 2 of II d.44 treats the power of ruling. Every ruling power is from God as to its essence, a divinely instituted order of superior to inferior for praising the good and punishing evildoers. Its unjust acquisition and abuse are only permitted by God, so a usurped power can be wrongly seized yet divinely conferred under different respects. On the state of innocence, Richard distinguishes dominion as ownership and use, as directive command and as coercion. The first two would have existed, the second only within the household, but coercion is a consequence of sin and will vanish in glory.
claims: Political power is from God in its essence but only permissively in unjust acquisition and abuse.
Coercive dominion arises from the Fall.
Directive household authority existed in innocence.
